answer.rationale: The binding constraint is timing, not opportunity: the contract lapses in 14 days and the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. That rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle — memory_c2 is explicit that the low-cost vendor missed SLA in three of four quarters, and a migration under zero slack converts a cost win into a delivery failure. It also weakens defer_decision (memory_c5 applied to a non-critical renewal on month-to-month terms; this is a critical line with no such fallback). add_second_source is the right structural move and memory_c3 supports it, but qualification takes longer than 14 days and it does not by itself deliver the 18% spend cut. That leaves negotiating with the incumbent, where memory_c4 (benchmarking moved price and payment terms) and memory_c6 (multi-year unlocked volume pricing without narrowing scope) are the two load-bearing claims — so those are the two I verify. I want the original records because both are the kind of memory that gets compressed favorably: c4 may not record how much of the 'real margin' was price versus one-time concessions, and c6 may not record what the incumbent extracted for the longer term. Risk I am flagging downstream: an 18% mandate creates pressure to buy the cut with a long lock-in or by quietly consolidating to the cheap vendor later; a multi-year commitment signed under this pressure removes the flexibility needed to add the second source next cycle, which is the actual fix for single-point-of-failure. So I will negotiate for price and payment terms with the shortest term that clears the target, explicitly preserving the right to dual-source, rather than trading term length for the full discount. Confidence is in the direction, not the magnitude: whether negotiation alone reaches 18% is unknown until the archived records show what was actually recovered, and if it falls short the honest answer is a partial cut plus second-source qualification next review, not a riskier switch.
